1	# Per-paper extraction instructions, v6 (GP-RareLink; Claude Code route, D-20)
2	
3	*Changes from v2 come from the Stage 3 findings (`reports/poc_stage3_findings.md`) and decision D-22, marked "(v3)". Changes from v3 come from the Stage 3b findings (`reports/poc_stage3b_findings.md`) and decisions D-23 and D-24, marked "(v4)". The changes from v4 are D-27 and D-29 (Jimmy, 2026-10-19), from the Stage 5 audit (`reports/poc_stage4_5_findings.md` §10), marked "(v5)". v5 was checked on 20 HA20 papers under D-29 (`poc-ha20-v5-subset`). The change from v5 is D-31 (Jimmy, 2026-10-19), from the re-audit (`reports/poc_stage4_5_findings.md` §10.7), marked "(v6)": no positional reading of stacked cells. v6 is the candidate for the frozen pipeline; it has not been run.*
4	
5	You extract structured evidence from **one** published paper for a literature-curation study of A20 haploinsufficiency (HA20), the disease caused by germline *TNFAIP3* variants. Your output is checked by script (every quote must be found verbatim in the paper) and then by a separate reviewer, so accuracy and honest abstention matter more than completeness.
6	
7	## Inputs (paths are given in your task)
8	
9	1. **The paper**: a Markdown file converted from the PMC or Europe PMC full text. Its first lines give the PMID and title. Merged table cells are repeated in every row and column they cover.
10	   - **(v3)** The file may end with a `## Supplementary material` section converted from the files published with the article. Treat it as part of the paper and quote it verbatim like any other text.
11	   - Some supplementary files are excerpts, with `[...]` marking omitted lines. Never join text across `[...]`.
12	   - **(v4)** In tables converted from supplementary files, ` / ` separates values that were stacked on separate lines inside one cell (see "Stacked cells" below; changed in v6).
13	2. **The schema**: `pipeline/extract/claude_code/schema_ha20_v5.json`. It defines five tables, their fields, types, allowed values, and a description for each.
14	3. **The rules**: `pipeline/extract/sliders_adapter/prompts/extraction_rules_v1.md`. Apply all nine. Where this file is more specific (scope, labels, table symbols), this file wins.
15	
16	**What you may read.** Read only these three files.
17	- Do not open any other file in the repository.
18	- Do not use web search or web fetch.
19	- Do not use anything you remember about this paper, its authors, its patients, the gene or the variants.
20	
21	**What counts as missing.** If the paper doesn't say it, the value is missing (see "Values" below).
22	
23	## Scope: who gets a row (v3, D-22)
24	
25	- **In scope:**
26	  - every person the paper describes who has a *TNFAIP3* variant or an HA20 (A20 haploinsufficiency) diagnosis;
27	  - relatives the paper describes in relation to such a person, whether tested (including tested negative) or affected.
28	- **Out of scope:** other members of a cohort, for example patients whose variants are in other genes, or who have no variant. They get **no** rows. Record the study's total number of patients, as the authors state it, in `publications.cohort_size_as_stated`.
29	- **People from summaries of earlier reports are in scope** when they meet the rule above: a literature table in a case report, or a review describing individuals. Each gets its own row, with `source_reference_in_review` filled verbatim.
30	  - **(v4)** A previously published person mentioned only in passing (for example one sentence in the Discussion) is in scope only when the paper gives at least one individual-level fact about that person beyond the diagnosis: sex, age, variant or a feature.
31	  - **(v4, D-23)** When a table has a per-patient reference or source column, copy that cell into `source_reference_in_review` for each patient, also in cohort and survey papers. Do not leave it only in `method_note`; the cross-paper merge depends on it.
32	- **Variants in other genes:**
33	  - record one only for an in-scope person, and only when the paper attributes it to that person unambiguously;
34	  - do not list risk alleles or polygenic-score variants;
35	  - **(v4)** do not create a row for a variant the paper names but does not describe (no printed variant), for example "variants in PIK3R1 and HBB";
36	  - if the attribution is contradictory, leave it out and say so in `method_note`.
37	- **(v4) Other variant rows to leave out:** common variants the authors dismiss as non-causal (for example a frequent SNP they call benign), and variants found only in tumour tissue (somatic).
38	- **(v4) Mosaic carriers:** a person with a germline mosaic *TNFAIP3* variant is in scope; record zygosity `mosaic`.
39	- **`reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant`** is `true` only when the paper describes at least one identifiable in-scope person, that is, with any individual-level detail. A paper that mentions such patients only as counts or at group level gets `false`.
40	
41	## Labels (v3, D-22)
42	
43	Choose each person's `individual_label_in_paper` by the first rule that applies, so that two independent extractions give the same label:
44	1. **The paper's own label**, verbatim, in the form it uses most often (e.g. `P1`, `Patient 3`, `II-2`).
45	2. **A relative without an own label:** `<relation as written> of <label of the related person>` (e.g. `mother of P1`, `sister of patient`).
46	3. **A table row without a label column:** `Table <n> row <k>`, with k counting data rows from the top (e.g. `Table 2 row 3`).
47	4. **A previously published person described in the text without a label:** `ref <reference as printed> patient` (e.g. `ref [12] patient`). Add ` 2`, ` 3` for further people from the same reference, in order of mention.
48	5. **The single unnamed patient of a case report:** `patient`.
49	6. **Otherwise:** `unnamed person <k>`, in order of first mention.
50	
51	**(v4) Additions:**
52	- **Patients as table columns:** `Table <n> column <k>`, with k counting data columns from the left.
53	- **A table column of bare numbers that index the patients** (values like 1, 2, 3 under a heading such as "No.", "Case" or "Patient number"): `Table <n> #<value>` (e.g. `Table 3 #1`). If the values are labels such as "P1" or "Case 2", or the text uses its own label for that person, rule 1 applies.
54	- **The same label in two families** (e.g. two people called "IV:1"): `<label> (Family <n>)`.
55	- **Role words are not labels.** "The proband", "the index case" or "our patient" do not count as the paper's own label; use rule 5 or 6.
56	- **Relatives without a stated sex:** when the paper says only "parents", "children" or "siblings", write `parent of X`, `child of X` or `sibling of X` (and `parent of X 2` for the second). Never guess "mother" or "brother".
57	- A made-up label (rules 3–6) still needs a span: quote the text where the person first appears.
58	
59	Use the identical label in every table for the same person.
60	
61	## Output: one JSON file, at the path given in your task
62	
63	```json
64	{
65	  "pmid": "<from the paper's header line>",
66	  "instructions_version": "extract_v6",
67	  "reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant": true,
68	  "relevance_note": "<one sentence, with a short quote, saying why>",
69	  "method_note": "<how you worked, e.g. whether a script transcribed a table; list any contradictions you found in the paper>",
70	  "tables": {
71	    "publications": [ROW],
72	    "individuals": [ROW, ...],
73	    "variants": [ROW, ...],
74	    "phenotypic_features": [ROW, ...],
75	    "phenotype_checklist": [ROW, ...]
76	  }
77	}
78	```
79	
80	A **ROW** is an object with every field of that table, using the field names exactly as in the schema. Each field maps to a **cell**:
81	
82	```json
83	{"value": <value>, "span": "<exact quote from the paper>"}
84	```
85	
86	### Values
87	- **Type.** Use the schema's type for each field. Enum fields take only the listed strings.
88	- **Missing values.** Follow each field's schema description.
89	  - Where the description says "null", use `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
90	  - Otherwise, text and enum fields take `{"value": "not reported", "span": null}`, and numeric, date and boolean fields take `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
91	- **`pmid` fields.** The value comes from the header line; the span is that header line, e.g. `"PMID: 12345678"`.
92	- **`*_iso8601` fields.** These are your conversion of the matching original-text field. Give them only when the original text states a number, and use the same span as the original-text field.
93	- **`hpo_label_candidate` and `hpo_id_candidate`.** These are your suggestions. Give an ID only if you are sure of it; otherwise null. Their span is `null`.
94	- **`checklist_feature`.** The span is `null`, because the names come from the schema.
95	- **Age at diagnosis.** Record it in `age_at_diagnosis_*`. Don't put it in onset or last evaluation.
96	
97	### Spans
98	- **Every non-missing value needs a span**, except the fields listed just above.
99	- **Copy exactly.** A span is copied character for character from the paper Markdown, including unusual spaces and symbols. Never paraphrase, correct or join text that isn't contiguous.
100	- **Keep it short.** Use the smallest sentence fragment, table cell or table-row segment that supports the value. That is normally under 300 characters.
101	- **Tables with patients as rows.** Quote a contiguous piece of the row from the patient label through the cell.
102	- **Tables with patients as columns.** Quote the row from its row label through that patient's cell, e.g. `| Sex | F | M` for the second patient column. Name the column header once in `method_note`.
103	- **Multiple places.** If support sits in several places, `span` may be a list of exact quotes:
104	  - up to **five** for `treatment_summary`, `functional_evidence_statement`, `parental_testing_statement` and `clinical_diagnosis_basis`;
105	  - up to **three** for any other field.
106	
107	### Rows
108	- **`publications`:** exactly one row for this paper.
109	- **`individuals`:** one row per in-scope person (see Scope), labelled by the Labels rules.
110	- **`variants`:** one row per (person, variant).
111	  - `variant_original_string` is the **shortest** contiguous text giving the variant, not a whole sentence. Put the transcript, cDNA and protein parts in their own fields.
112	  - **(v3)** If the paper ties a *TNFAIP3* variant to the person but prints no variant description (only in a figure or an unavailable supplement), keep the row with `variant_original_string` = `"not reported"`. Never fill it from memory.
113	- **`phenotypic_features`:** one row per feature the paper explicitly reports present (`observed`) or explicitly reports absent (`excluded`) for that person. No rows for features the paper doesn't mention.
114	- **`phenotype_checklist`:** for **every** individual, one row for **each** of the 20 checklist features in the schema's description of that table, using the names exactly as listed there. Status is `observed`, `excluded` or `not reported` under rule 4.
115	
116	### Absence and evidence basis (D-21, D-22)
117	- **`evidence_basis` is required** on every `phenotypic_features` row, and on every checklist row whose status is not `not reported`.
118	- **Group statements.** You may mark a feature `excluded` for a person from a statement about a group **only when the statement names the group explicitly**, e.g. "only Pt3 of the four patients had recurrent fevers". Such rows take `evidence_basis = "inferred from group statement"`.
119	  - Counts without names ("arthritis in 2/4") do not exclude anyone.
120	- **(v3) Table symbols.** A `-`, `–`, `0`, `N` or similar cell counts as `excluded` only when the paper's legend or text defines that symbol as absent or negative.
121	  - Quote that definition as a second span next to the cell.
122	  - Otherwise the cell is `not reported` (rule 6). Empty cells, `NA` and `ND` are always `not reported`.
123	- **(v3) Study criteria are not evidence.** Never use a study's inclusion or exclusion criteria (e.g. "patients with malignancy were excluded") to mark a feature for a person.
124	- **Narrow and broad features.** A narrower absence never excludes a broader checklist item. "No arthritis" does not exclude "arthritis or arthralgia"; leave that item `not reported` unless arthralgia is also addressed. The same applies to other composite items, e.g. "skin lesions (rash, folliculitis, erythema nodosum)".
125	- **(v5, D-27) Normal findings.** When the paper reports a finding as normal or negative for a person ("CRP was normal", "normal C3 and C4 levels", "ANA negative"), record the abnormality it rules out as the feature and mark it `excluded`: `feature_text_as_stated` = "elevated CRP", "low complement", "positive ANA". Keep the paper's own words in the span ("CRP was normal"). Name only an abnormality the finding measures; a normal examination or investigation as a whole ("gastrointestinal investigation was negative") excludes nothing more specific than what it names, so write it as the paper does and say so in `method_note`.
126	- **(v4) Zero counts.** A count of 0 in a table of counts (e.g. "0" or "0/2" in a column for a disease group) excludes no one, like any count without names. Text that names the group ("none of the patients had uveitis") still excludes.
127	- **(v6, D-31) Stacked cells.** A cell with several values separated by ` / ` lists values that were stacked on separate lines (often one per patient). **Do not assign them to people by position**, even when the number of values equals the number of people. Use a stacked value for a person only when the paper labels it for that person (for example "P1: 18 / P2: 24", or a sentence naming the person and the value). Otherwise record the field or checklist item as `not reported` for each person in that row, and say in `method_note` which table and columns were stacked. A value the same for every person in the row, printed once (not stacked), is not affected.
128	- **Contradictions inside the paper.** If the paper says both that a person has a feature and that they don't:
129	  - emit both `phenotypic_features` rows, each with its own span;
130	  - set that checklist item to `not reported`;
131	  - list the contradiction in `method_note`.
132	
133	### Variant fields belong to this person's variant (v5, D-29)
134	Zygosity, inheritance, variant type, pathogenicity, ACMG criteria and functional evidence describe **one person's variant**. Fill them only from:
135	- this person's own table row or column, or a sentence that names this person or this exact variant; or
136	- a statement about a **named group that includes this person** and gives one value for all of them ("all six patients carried heterozygous variants").
137	
138	Leave the field `not reported` (with span null) when:
139	- the statement is about the cohort's or the paper's variants in general, without naming a group this person is clearly in ("the variants were classified as pathogenic");
140	- the statement lists several values for a group ("splice-site, frameshift and nonsense variants"): it does not say which one is this person's;
141	- the paper gives this person a different or open status elsewhere: a variant not identified or not determined, a mosaic or somatic finding, a VUS, a relative not tested. A group statement never overrides that;
142	- the value is about another person's variant, for example a relative carrying the proband's variant, unless the paper says it for the relative.
143	
144	Variant type: record only a class the paper states for this variant (or for a named group of variants that includes it). Do not derive it from the HGVS string.
145	
146	### Inheritance (v4, D-24)
147	- **De novo:** only when the paper states parental testing with the variant absent in both parents (rule 8).
148	- **Inherited:** record `inherited maternal` or `inherited paternal` when the paper states that the named parent carries the same variant, even if it never uses the word "inherited". Quote that statement in `parental_testing_statement`. Use `inherited unspecified parent` when it says a parent carries it without saying which.
149	- **Otherwise:** `not reported`. Do not infer from a pedigree drawing or from an affected but untested parent.
150	- This is more specific than rule 8, so it wins.
151	
152	### When the paper describes no in-scope person
153	For example, a review without patient-level detail, or a paper about something else:
154	- set `reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant` to `false`;
155	- fill the `publications` row;
156	- leave the other tables empty.

158	### Large papers
159	If the output is long, you may build it in parts with a short Python script and combine the parts.
160	- Every value must still come from your reading of the paper.
161	- If a script transcribes a table, check its output against the table and say so in `method_note`.
162	- Use only your own scratch directory (given in your task) for temporary files.

1	Extraction rules (GP-RareLink, v1). These rules apply to every table and every row.
2	
3	1. Use only the supplied document. Do not use outside knowledge about the gene, the disease, specific variants or specific patients. If the document does not state something, the value is "not reported" (for text fields) or null (for numeric and date fields). Never fill a gap from memory.
4	2. Every value must be supported by a verbatim quote copied exactly from the document. Do not paraphrase inside the quote. If no exact quote supports a value, do not emit the value.
5	3. Keep original strings. Record variant descriptions, ages, feature names and labels exactly as printed. Never convert protein-only variant descriptions into cDNA notation, never add a transcript that is not printed, never translate units.
6	4. Three-state phenotypes: a feature is "observed" only when the document says the person has or had it, and "excluded" only when the document explicitly says it was absent, negative or not found in that person. Silence is "not reported". Never turn silence into "excluded".
7	5. One row per real person per document. Relatives described in the document are their own rows with is_proband = false unless the document calls them probands. Do not merge people, and do not create a person the document does not describe.
8	6. Cohort tables: when a table lists many patients, extract each patient row separately with the table's own patient identifier as individual_label_in_paper. Keep the row-to-column alignment of the table; when a cell is empty or marked "-", "NA" or "ND", treat it as not reported.
9	7. Re-reports: if the document says that any of its patients were described in an earlier publication, record that statement and the citation in the publications table. Do not drop the patient.
10	8. Do not infer inheritance or zygosity. "de novo" requires that the document states parental testing showed the variant absent in both parents. "heterozygous" requires that the document says so or the gene is described as monoallelic for that person.
11	9. Prefer "not reported" to a plausible guess. Abstention is correct behaviour.

1	PMID: 38183052
2	PMCID: PMC10770963
3	DOI: 10.1186/s12969-023-00947-z
4	Title: A20 haploinsufficiency in a neonate caused by a large deletion on chromosome 6q
5	Journal: Pediatric Rheumatology Online Journal (2024)
6	Authors: Zhang Fan; Zhang Liang
7	
8	# A20 haploinsufficiency in a neonate caused by a large deletion on chromosome 6q
9	
10	## Abstract
11	
12	AbstractHaploinsufficiency of A20 (HA20) is a rare monogenic disease caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the tumor necrosis factor alpha-induced protein 3 (TNFAIP3) gene located on chromosome 6q23.3. The majority of disease-causing mutations in most cases of HA20 comprise single nucleotide variations, small insertions, or deletions in TNFAIP3, which result in a premature termination codon and subsequent disruption of its anti-inflammatory role. Large deletions have been reported sporadically. HA20 patients may present with a variety of autoinflammatory and autoimmune features during early childhood; however, cases with neonatal onset are rare. Here, we describe a Chinese neonate presenting with concomitant inflammatory and other syndromic manifestations caused by a 5.15 Mb interstitial deletion in chromosome 6; these deletions affect TNFAIP3. Taken together, the data extend the clinical and genetic spectra of HA20.Keywords: A20 haploinsufficiency, Chromosome deletion, Autoinflammatory, Neonate
13	
14	## Background
15	
16	Heterozygous pathogenic mutations in the gene encoding tumor necrosis factor alpha-induced protein 3 (TNFAIP3) result in haploinsufficiency of A20 (HA20), a rare hereditary autoinflammatory disease [1–3]. The TNFAIP3 gene, located on chromosome 6q23.3, encodes the A20 protein, which acts as a central gatekeeper for negative regulation of NF-κB signaling, NLRP3 inflammasome activity, and apoptosis [4, 5]. HA20 is characterized typically by various autoinflammatory features that resemble Behçet’s disease, or by autoimmune symptoms that mimic systemic lupus erythematosus, or correlated with allergy-associated features [1, 6–9]. So far, more than one hundred HA20 patients have been reported in the literature, and the majority of TNFAIP3 variants are monoallelic nonsense and frameshift mutations, small insertions, or small deletions; the disease commonly manifests in early childhood [10–12]. However, cases with neonatal onset and/or caused by copy number variations resulting from large contiguous gene deletions of 6q involving the TNFAIP3 gene are rare. Here, we described a neonate presenting with concomitant inflammatory and other syndromic manifestations caused by a 5.15 Mb interstitial deletion on chromosome 6.
17	
18	## Clinical report
19	
20	The neonate was born to a 29-year-old mother via in vitro fertilization. She was preterm (delivered, at a gestational age of 36 weeks, by cesarean section) and weighed 2700 g. There was no consanguinity, significant family history of immunodeficiency, or abnormalities detected during pregnancy. She presented with decreased activity and clear growth delay. Since the age of 23 days, she suffered from recurrent episodes of low to moderate-grade fever (37.6–39℃) one to three times per day. She was treated preliminarily with antibiotics, including amoxicillin/potassium clavulanate followed by cefotaxime for two weeks, but the febrile attack did not subside immediately; rather, it resolved gradually within 24 days (Fig. 1a).
21	
22	**Fig. 1**: Clinical manifestations and genetic characteristics. A Daily maximum core temperature in the neonate from Day 23 post-birth. B Hemoglobin (g/L) levels measured during febrile episodes, as well as basal levels measured at birth and follow-up (green arrows denote infusions of hemoglobin). C Circulating concentrations of alanine transaminase (ALT; IU/L, blue quadrangle) and aspartate transaminase (AST; IU/L, purple triangle) over time. D Fluctuation of blood serum CMV-DNA levels (10^3 copies/mL); the black arrow indicates initiation of ganciclovir treatment. E A large deletion in chromosome 6 and OMIM genes encompassing the 6q23.2q24.3 region
23	
24	On admission, extrauterine growth restricted was noted. Body weight and head circumference were below the 3rd and 10th percentiles, respectively. Physical examination revealed enlarged liver and spleen, 4 cm below the right costal margin and 2.5 cm below the left costal margin, respectively. Blood analysis revealed slightly elevated white blood cell counts, and C-reactive protein levels, which gradually returned to normal levels accompanied by extinguished fever within 22 days. She suffered worsening of her acute severe anemia with elevated percent of reticulocyte up to 3.87% gradually after the onset of fever (Fig. 1b). However, there was no clear evidence of hemoglobin loss or hemolysis, without clinical signs of active bleeding or jaundice; routine test of urine, feces and kidney function were normal without hyperbilirubinemia or increased serum lactate dehydrogenase; direct antiglobulin test, hemoglobin analysis, red cell osmotic fragility test and enzymatic activity test of G6PD were negative. Liver enzymes were elevated constantly for 10 days after onset of the febrile attacks (Fig. 1c). No immunosuppressive treatment rather than regular project therapy was given, however, the ameliorative level of liver enzymes and anemia was correlated with gradual resolution of febrile attack. Mild anemia and hepatic injury reappeared after another slight fever lasting for about one week (Fig. 1b, c).
25	
26	Measurement of autoantibodies, anti-toxoplasma gondii, Rubella Virus, Cytomegalovirus, and Herpes simplex virus (TORCH) were normal. Pathogen cultures were negative, as well as tandem mass spectrometry and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry for screening particular inheritance metabolism diseases. No other obvious abnormalities were found in ophthalmologic assessment, hearing test and brain MRI scans. Abdominal ultrasonography showed no other abnormalitis except for hepatomegaly.
27	
28	Metagenomic next generation sequencing was performed to detect pathogenic agents, which showed CMV positive, and PCR detected cytomegalovirus (CMV) DNA in the serum, she was given ganciclovir for two weeks (Fig. 1d). An unexpected discovery was that the metagenomic next generation sequencing simultaneously prompted genomic deletions. In light of this surprise tip, analysis of copy number variations were performed using a comparative genomic hybridization array and revealed a heterozygous 5.15 Mb deletion in 6q23.3q24.3 (Fig. 1e). The deletion affected at least 30 genes, including TNFAIP3. Finally, she was definitively diagnosed with HA20.
29	
30	She subsequently experienced developmental delay in motor, and also presented growth retardation since the age of six months, at that time, ameliorated hepatomegaly was revealed as enlarged liver was 3 cm below the right costal margin, and her spleen was not palpable. The COVID-19 epidemic led to suspension of her out-patient clinics and follow-up visits.
31	
32	## Literature review
33	
34	An English language search of the PubMed database was conducted up until 31st August 2023; the aim was to identify studies reporting clinical features of patients with HA20 caused by contiguous deletions of 6q including TNFAIP3.
35	
36	## Results
37	
38	At present, only 11 patients with HA20 molecularly confirmed to be caused by deletion of chromosome 6q have been reported since 2016 [13–20]. The initial clinical characteristics and genetic evaluation of all 12 patients are summarized in Table 1 and Fig. 2. Of all patients, eigtht were female, and five presented with de novo deletions on chromosome 6q. Nine patients experienced early-onset symptoms before the age of 1 year old; in seven patients, the initial symptoms were unprovoked and recurrent episodes of fever. Additionally, dysmorphic features and intellectual disability were reported sporadically, contributing to the complex phenotype. Intriguingly, it was assumed that the symptoms of HA20 may depend on genetic background and environmental factors; indeed, patients with A20 mutations widely distributed from the OTU to the ZnF7 domains from East Asia presented more frequently with recurrent fever [12]. Correspondingly, to some extent, unprovoked and recurrent episodes of fever as the initial symptoms were slightly more frequently observed in these patients from East Asia harboring deletion of 6q involving the TNFAIP3 gene. More cases are warranted to consolidate this phenomenon.
39

65	
66	## Discussion
67	
68	In this report, we presented a Chinese HA20 neonate presenting with concomitant inflammatory and other syndromic manifestations caused by a 5.15 Mb interstitial deletion in chromosome 6. We also reviewed the literature to include cases of patients with HA20 caused by contiguous deletions of 6q including TNFAIP3. In total, 12 cases have been reported to date. Most of the patients were from East Asia and presented with recurrent fever before the age of 1 year old. It has been considered that diagnosis of HA20 is challenging due to its heterogeneous clinical presentation and the lack of pathognomonic symptoms, especially in neonates and infants. Recurrent stomatitis is the most common symptom in HA20 patients caused by single nucleotide variations, small insertions, or small deletions in TNFAIP3. In contrast, our result and other literature show that in HA20 patients resulting from contiguous deletions of 6q including TNFAIP3, unprovoked and recurrent episodes of fever tends to be the most common symptom. Thus, HA20 should not be neglected and should be considered in the differential diagnosis of newborns and infants with recurrent episodes of fever.
69	
70	The zinc finger protein A20, a unique and potent regulator of ubiquitin (Ub)-dependent signaling encoded by the TNFAIP3 gene located on chromosome 6q23.3, plays a vital role in the immune homeostasis. A20 functions as a ubiquitin-editing enzyme (deubiquitinase [DUB]) that inhibits key proinflammatory molecules and protects cells from death [21]. This is attributed mainly to its role in modulating nuclear factor kappa B (NF-kB) signaling cascades as part of its key function as a negative regulator of inflammation and immune responses. A20 inhibits not only tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-dependent activation of nuclear factor (NF)-kB, but also the activation of NF-kB in response to interleukin (IL)-1; it also inhibits signaling cascades mediated through pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) and T cell and B cell antigen receptors; These cascades control crucial stages of immune cell homeostasis, including apoptosis, necroptosis, and inflammasome activity [22–24].
71	
72	Thus, A20 is a potent anti-inflammatory molecule. Indeed, mice harboring targeted cell-specific deletions in the TNFAIP3 gene in innate immune cells develop autoinflammatory diseases spontaneously, and mice harboring targeted cell-specific deletions in adaptive immune cells develop spontaneous inflammation that resembles human autoimmune diseases [24]. Actually, A20 has attracted attention due to its multiple links to a variety of human diseases. Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the A20 gene locus, which reduce expression of A20, were identified initially as putative risk alleles for a range of inflammatory and autoimmune pathologies, including rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, and systemic lupus erythematosus [25].
73	
74	In 2016, a new autoinflammatory disease presenting as an early-onset autoinflammatory condition resembling Behçet’s disease (BD), and caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the TNFAIP3 gene, was described and named A20 haploinsufficiency (HA20) [1]. Since then, numerous cases with a broad spectrum of clinical presentations associated with autoinflammatory syndromes, autoimmune diseases, and immunodeficiency have been reported worldwide. To date, more than one hundred HA20 patients have been reported in the literature, particularly in East Asian countries such China and Japan [10–12, 26]. The majority of TNFAIP3 variants harbor monoallelic nonsense and frameshift mutations, small insertions, and small deletions, leading to a premature termination codon and disrupted anti-inflammatory effects [10–12]. Overall, HA20 patients caused by copy number variations resulting from contiguous deletions of 6q (involving the TNFAIP3 gene) are rare [13–20]. Correspondingly, in clinical practice, the major phenotypes of HA20 caused by truncating and missense mutations are Behçet’s disease-like symptoms, with recurrent oral ulcers as the primary incipient sign, or autoimmune-like symptoms that mimic systemic lupus erythematosus, autoimmune thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes, autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA), and autoimmune hepatitis [12]. Until now, systematic correlation between the contiguous deletions of 6q and disease diagnosis has been far unavailable, actually, the diagnosis and management tends to be complicated in those caused by copy number variants involving the TNFAIP3 gene [19].
75	
76	The neonate in our study initially presented with unprovoked and long-lerm fever, associated with no apparently infectious manifestation, furthermore, adequate antibiotics therapy was administered without significant efficiency against the fever. It appeared that the fever was not attributed to the CMV infection as the resolution of fever had revealed before ganciclovir therapy initiation.
77	
78	It is also established that A20 is a crucial hepatoprotective factor in mice; indeed, A20 knockout resulted in excessive multi-organ inflammation (including the liver) [5]. Moreover, hepatocyte-specific A20 knockout mice showed sustained activation of NF-κB-dependent genes and increased apoptosis of hepatocytes, which was associated with liver failure [27, 28]. Additionally, dendritic cells-specific A20 knockout mice resulted in liver pathology characterized by inflammatory infiltrates adjacent to the portal triads [29]. As a consequence, elevated liver enzymes have been reported in HA20 patients with mutations in either the ZnF- or OTU-coding regions [10, 30].
79	
80	Our patient is the first reported case of a large deletion of 6q to present with liver injury. Furthermore, anemia caused by iron deficiency and AIHA has been reported in patients with HA20, which was not in accordance with our patient. Notably, A20 Hem-KO mice develop anemia due to a striking reduction of erythropoiesis in the bone marrow mediated pathophysiologically by IFN-γ [31, 32], which could partly interpret acute anemia in our patient.
81	
82	As mentioned above, HA20 caused by this large deletion in 6q is likely responsible for the recurrent fever and continuous liver injury, as well as acute anemia and hepatosplenomegaly, notwithstanding that CMV infection might complicate matters.
83	
84	## Conclusion
85	
86	Here, we describe for the first time a neonate presenting with concomitant complicated features caused by a large genomic deletion on chromosome 6q.
87

38	At present, only 11 patients with HA20 molecularly confirmed to be caused by deletion of chromosome 6q have been reported since 2016 [13–20]. The initial clinical characteristics and genetic evaluation of all 12 patients are summarized in Table 1 and Fig. 2. Of all patients, eigtht were female, and five presented with de novo deletions on chromosome 6q. Nine patients experienced early-onset symptoms before the age of 1 year old; in seven patients, the initial symptoms were unprovoked and recurrent episodes of fever. Additionally, dysmorphic features and intellectual disability were reported sporadically, contributing to the complex phenotype. Intriguingly, it was assumed that the symptoms of HA20 may depend on genetic background and environmental factors; indeed, patients with A20 mutations widely distributed from the OTU to the ZnF7 domains from East Asia presented more frequently with recurrent fever [12]. Correspondingly, to some extent, unprovoked and recurrent episodes of fever as the initial symptoms were slightly more frequently observed in these patients from East Asia harboring deletion of 6q involving the TNFAIP3 gene. More cases are warranted to consolidate this phenomenon.

68	In this report, we presented a Chinese HA20 neonate presenting with concomitant inflammatory and other syndromic manifestations caused by a 5.15 Mb interstitial deletion in chromosome 6. We also reviewed the literature to include cases of patients with HA20 caused by contiguous deletions of 6q including TNFAIP3. In total, 12 cases have been reported to date. Most of the patients were from East Asia and presented with recurrent fever before the age of 1 year old. It has been considered that diagnosis of HA20 is challenging due to its heterogeneous clinical presentation and the lack of pathognomonic symptoms, especially in neonates and infants. Recurrent stomatitis is the most common symptom in HA20 patients caused by single nucleotide variations, small insertions, or small deletions in TNFAIP3. In contrast, our result and other literature show that in HA20 patients resulting from contiguous deletions of 6q including TNFAIP3, unprovoked and recurrent episodes of fever tends to be the most common symptom. Thus, HA20 should not be neglected and should be considered in the differential diagnosis of newborns and infants with recurrent episodes of fever.

24	On admission, extrauterine growth restricted was noted. Body weight and head circumference were below the 3rd and 10th percentiles, respectively. Physical examination revealed enlarged liver and spleen, 4 cm below the right costal margin and 2.5 cm below the left costal margin, respectively. Blood analysis revealed slightly elevated white blood cell counts, and C-reactive protein levels, which gradually returned to normal levels accompanied by extinguished fever within 22 days. She suffered worsening of her acute severe anemia with elevated percent of reticulocyte up to 3.87% gradually after the onset of fever (Fig. 1b). However, there was no clear evidence of hemoglobin loss or hemolysis, without clinical signs of active bleeding or jaundice; routine test of urine, feces and kidney function were normal without hyperbilirubinemia or increased serum lactate dehydrogenase; direct antiglobulin test, hemoglobin analysis, red cell osmotic fragility test and enzymatic activity test of G6PD were negative. Liver enzymes were elevated constantly for 10 days after onset of the febrile attacks (Fig. 1c). No immunosuppressive treatment rather than regular project therapy was given, however, the ameliorative level of liver enzymes and anemia was correlated with gradual resolution of febrile attack. Mild anemia and hepatic injury reappeared after another slight fever lasting for about one week (Fig. 1b, c).
26	Measurement of autoantibodies, anti-toxoplasma gondii, Rubella Virus, Cytomegalovirus, and Herpes simplex virus (TORCH) were normal. Pathogen cultures were negative, as well as tandem mass spectrometry and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry for screening particular inheritance metabolism diseases. No other obvious abnormalities were found in ophthalmologic assessment, hearing test and brain MRI scans. Abdominal ultrasonography showed no other abnormalitis except for hepatomegaly.

20	The neonate was born to a 29-year-old mother via in vitro fertilization. She was preterm (delivered, at a gestational age of 36 weeks, by cesarean section) and weighed 2700 g. There was no consanguinity, significant family history of immunodeficiency, or abnormalities detected during pregnancy. She presented with decreased activity and clear growth delay. Since the age of 23 days, she suffered from recurrent episodes of low to moderate-grade fever (37.6–39℃) one to three times per day. She was treated preliminarily with antibiotics, including amoxicillin/potassium clavulanate followed by cefotaxime for two weeks, but the febrile attack did not subside immediately; rather, it resolved gradually within 24 days (Fig. 1a).
30	She subsequently experienced developmental delay in motor, and also presented growth retardation since the age of six months, at that time, ameliorated hepatomegaly was revealed as enlarged liver was 3 cm below the right costal margin, and her spleen was not palpable. The COVID-19 epidemic led to suspension of her out-patient clinics and follow-up visits.
80	Our patient is the first reported case of a large deletion of 6q to present with liver injury. Furthermore, anemia caused by iron deficiency and AIHA has been reported in patients with HA20, which was not in accordance with our patient. Notably, A20 Hem-KO mice develop anemia due to a striking reduction of erythropoiesis in the bone marrow mediated pathophysiologically by IFN-γ [31, 32], which could partly interpret acute anemia in our patient.

4	Title: A20 haploinsufficiency in a neonate caused by a large deletion on chromosome 6q
8	# A20 haploinsufficiency in a neonate caused by a large deletion on chromosome 6q
20	The neonate was born to a 29-year-old mother via in vitro fertilization. She was preterm (delivered, at a gestational age of 36 weeks, by cesarean section) and weighed 2700 g. There was no consanguinity, significant family history of immunodeficiency, or abnormalities detected during pregnancy. She presented with decreased activity and clear growth delay. Since the age of 23 days, she suffered from recurrent episodes of low to moderate-grade fever (37.6–39℃) one to three times per day. She was treated preliminarily with antibiotics, including amoxicillin/potassium clavulanate followed by cefotaxime for two weeks, but the febrile attack did not subside immediately; rather, it resolved gradually within 24 days (Fig. 1a).
22	**Fig. 1**: Clinical manifestations and genetic characteristics. A Daily maximum core temperature in the neonate from Day 23 post-birth. B Hemoglobin (g/L) levels measured during febrile episodes, as well as basal levels measured at birth and follow-up (green arrows denote infusions of hemoglobin). C Circulating concentrations of alanine transaminase (ALT; IU/L, blue quadrangle) and aspartate transaminase (AST; IU/L, purple triangle) over time. D Fluctuation of blood serum CMV-DNA levels (10^3 copies/mL); the black arrow indicates initiation of ganciclovir treatment. E A large deletion in chromosome 6 and OMIM genes encompassing the 6q23.2q24.3 region
24	On admission, extrauterine growth restricted was noted. Body weight and head circumference were below the 3rd and 10th percentiles, respectively. Physical examination revealed enlarged liver and spleen, 4 cm below the right costal margin and 2.5 cm below the left costal margin, respectively. Blood analysis revealed slightly elevated white blood cell counts, and C-reactive protein levels, which gradually returned to normal levels accompanied by extinguished fever within 22 days. She suffered worsening of her acute severe anemia with elevated percent of reticulocyte up to 3.87% gradually after the onset of fever (Fig. 1b). However, there was no clear evidence of hemoglobin loss or hemolysis, without clinical signs of active bleeding or jaundice; routine test of urine, feces and kidney function were normal without hyperbilirubinemia or increased serum lactate dehydrogenase; direct antiglobulin test, hemoglobin analysis, red cell osmotic fragility test and enzymatic activity test of G6PD were negative. Liver enzymes were elevated constantly for 10 days after onset of the febrile attacks (Fig. 1c). No immunosuppressive treatment rather than regular project therapy was given, however, the ameliorative level of liver enzymes and anemia was correlated with gradual resolution of febrile attack. Mild anemia and hepatic injury reappeared after another slight fever lasting for about one week (Fig. 1b, c).
28	Metagenomic next generation sequencing was performed to detect pathogenic agents, which showed CMV positive, and PCR detected cytomegalovirus (CMV) DNA in the serum, she was given ganciclovir for two weeks (Fig. 1d). An unexpected discovery was that the metagenomic next generation sequencing simultaneously prompted genomic deletions. In light of this surprise tip, analysis of copy number variations were performed using a comparative genomic hybridization array and revealed a heterozygous 5.15 Mb deletion in 6q23.3q24.3 (Fig. 1e). The deletion affected at least 30 genes, including TNFAIP3. Finally, she was definitively diagnosed with HA20.
